parts.title: The bridge in my town
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
My father is an engineer, and he builds bridges. When I was small, I thought this was the best job in the world, and I still think so. Our town has one very old bridge across the river, and he says that it is the most beautiful one in the country.

The bridge is made of grey stone and has five arches. It was built more than two hundred years ago, without any machines, by workers who carried every stone by hand. Every year, thousands of tourists come to take photographs of it, and in summer, children jump into the river from its low wall, although this is not allowed.

Last winter, there was a very big flood, and the river rose almost to the top of the arches. Everyone in the town was afraid that the bridge would fall. My father and his team worked day and night to check it, and in the end, it survived without a single crack.

When I told my teacher about this, she asked me to write about it for school. I wrote that old bridges are like old people: they have seen many things, and they are stronger than they look.

questions.prompt: What does the writer think about her father's job?
options: It is the best job in the world
It is too difficult for most people
It takes him away from the family
questions.explanation: She thought, and still thinks, that it is the best job in the world.

questions.prompt: How was the bridge built?
options: By workers who carried the stones
With the help of big machines
By a team of foreign engineers
questions.explanation: Workers carried every stone by hand, without any machines.

questions.prompt: What do some children do in the summer?
options: They jump from the bridge wall
questions.explanation: Children jump into the river from its low wall.

questions.prompt: What happened to the bridge during the flood?
options: It lost one of its arches
It was closed for a long time
It was not damaged at all
questions.explanation: It survived without a single crack.

questions.prompt: What did the writer say in her school work?
options: Floods are a great danger to towns
Old bridges are stronger than they look
questions.explanation: She wrote that old bridges are stronger than they look.

parts.title: The race to the sky
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There is one extra sentence.
parts.passage:
For hundreds of years, the tallest buildings in the world were churches and towers. Then, at the end of the nineteenth century, a new kind of building appeared in the United States: the skyscraper. [1] Two things made this possible: steel and the lift.

Steel is much stronger than stone, so builders could make walls that were thinner and higher. [2] Before that invention, nobody wanted to live or work on the tenth floor, because the stairs were too tiring.

Soon, cities around the world began to compete. [3] Each new tower was taller than the last, and people loved to watch the cranes lift the steel high above the streets.

Today, the tallest skyscraper is more than eight hundred metres high. [4] It has more than a hundred and sixty floors, and the lift to the top takes about a minute.

Of course, tall buildings use a lot of energy. [5] Because of this, many architects now design towers with plants on the walls and solar panels on the roof.
sentences: The first examples were only about ten floors high.
The lift was just as important, because it carried people up quickly.
It is so tall that, on a clear day, it can be seen from a hundred kilometres away.
Paris, London and Dubai all wanted the highest tower.
People who live in cold climates prefer small houses.
This has become a serious worry for the planet.

gaps.explanation: The first examples were only ten floors high, which follows the arrival of the skyscraper and leads to steel and the lift.
The lift carried people up quickly, and the next sentence says nobody wanted to live on the tenth floor before.
Paris, London and Dubai wanted the highest tower, which describes cities competing.
The sentence about being seen from a hundred kilometres away describes the very tall skyscraper.
The worry for the planet follows the energy use, and the next sentence says architects now use plants and solar panels.

parts.title: Why bridges stay up
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: A bridge has to carry a very heavy load. Think of all the cars, lorries and people [1] cross it every day! To do this, engineers use a few clever ideas. The first one is the arch: in an old stone bridge, the weight is pushed to the sides and down [2] the ground. Modern bridges often hang from strong steel cables, which are like giant ropes. These cables are attached to tall towers, [3] hold most of the weight. Engineers also test every bridge with computers before they begin to build it. They want to be sure [4] it can survive strong winds and floods. A good bridge can stay in place for a hundred years or [5], and it only needs a little care. When you cross a bridge, [6] a moment to think about the people who designed it.

gaps.explanation: People who cross it: a relative pronoun for people.
The weight goes down into the ground at the sides.
Towers which hold most of the weight: a relative pronoun.
Be sure that it can survive: a clause after sure.
A hundred years or more means longer than a hundred years.
Take a moment to think: a common phrase.

parts.title: A talk about the Golden Gate Bridge
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note with one word.

turns.speaker: bernice
turns.text: Good morning, everyone. Today, I would like to tell you about one of the most famous bridges in the world, the Golden Gate Bridge in San Francisco. It opened in nineteen thirty-seven, after four years of building. The bridge is almost three kilometres long, and its two towers are more than two hundred metres high. You might be surprised to learn that the colour of the bridge is not gold. It is a bright orange-red, which engineers call international orange. The colour was chosen because it is easy to see in the thick fog that often covers the bay. About ten million cars cross the bridge every year, and many tourists walk or ride bicycles over it. Painters work on the bridge all year round to protect it from the salt in the air. If you ever visit, I recommend that you go in the morning, when the views are clearest.

gaps.prompt: The bridge opened in nineteen thirty-___
The towers are more than ___ metres high
gaps.explanation: More than two hundred metres high.

gaps.prompt: The colour is easy to see in the ___
gaps.explanation: Easy to see in the thick fog.

gaps.prompt: The best time to visit is in the ___
gaps.explanation: I recommend that you go in the morning.

parts.title: An interview with an architect
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Emeric, you design houses and public buildings. When did you decide to become an architect?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: When I was ten, I built a model of our house from cardboard. My parents kept it on a shelf for years, and I realised that I wanted to do this for a living.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What does an architect do all day?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: A lot of different things. I draw plans, but I also visit building sites, talk to clients and explain my ideas to the builders.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What makes a good building?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: It must be useful, safe and beautiful, in that order. If people do not feel happy inside a building, I have not done my job well.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What is the most difficult part?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Money. Clients always want to spend less, and I always want to use better materials. We have to find a balance.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Which of your buildings are you proudest of?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: A small school in a village in the mountains. The children helped to paint the walls, and now they say that it is theirs.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What advice would you give to a young person?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Look around you. Notice doors, windows and streets, and ask yourself why they look the way they do. That is the first lesson.
